claim: In yeast, the glucose-induced degradation-deficient (GID) E3 ligase selectively degrades superfluous gluconeogenic enzymes.
source: In yeast, the glucose-induced degradation-deficient (GID) E3 ligase selectively degrades superfluous gluconeogenic enzymes.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge of yeast GID function, supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: All subunits of the mammalian GID/CTLH complex have been identified.
source: Here, we identified all subunits of the mammalian GID/CTLH complex and provide a comprehensive map of its hierarchical organization and step-wise assembly.
evidence: This claim is supported by the AP-MS experiments and biochemical reconstitution data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mammalian GID/CTLH complex possesses inherent E3 ubiquitin ligase activity.
source: Biochemical reconstitution demonstrates that the mammalian complex possesses inherent E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, using Ube2H as its cognate E2.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro ubiquitination assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: Ube2H is the cognate E2 enzyme for the mammalian GID/CTLH complex.
source: Biochemical reconstitution demonstrates that the mammalian complex possesses inherent E3 ubiquitin ligase activity, using Ube2H as its cognate E2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays testing multiple E2 enzymes.

claim: Deletions of multiple GID subunits compromise cell proliferation.
source: Deletions of multiple GID subunits compromise cell proliferation, and this defect is accompanied by deregulation of critical cell cycle markers such as the retinoblastoma (Rb) tumor suppressor, phospho-Histone H3 and Cyclin A.
evidence: This is supported by clonogenic assays, MTT assays, and Western blot analysis of cell cycle markers.

claim: Deletion of GID subunits leads to deregulation of the retinoblastoma (Rb) tumor suppressor.
source: Deletions of multiple GID subunits compromise cell proliferation, and this defect is accompanied by deregulation of critical cell cycle markers such as the retinoblastoma (Rb) tumor suppressor, phospho-Histone H3 and Cyclin A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing altered Rb phosphorylation and levels.

claim: Deletion of GID subunits leads to deregulation of phospho-Histone H3.
source: Deletions of multiple GID subunits compromise cell proliferation, and this defect is accompanied by deregulation of critical cell cycle markers such as the retinoblastoma (Rb) tumor suppressor, phospho-Histone H3 and Cyclin A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing loss of phospho-Histone H3 in GID-KO cells.

claim: Deletion of GID subunits leads to deregulation of Cyclin A.
source: Deletions of multiple GID subunits compromise cell proliferation, and this defect is accompanied by deregulation of critical cell cycle markers such as the retinoblastoma (Rb) tumor suppressor, phospho-Histone H3 and Cyclin A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing reduced Cyclin A levels in GID-KO cells.

claim: Hbp1 is a bonafide GID/CTLH proteolytic substrate.
source: We identify the negative regulator of pro-proliferative genes Hbp1 as a bonafide GID/CTLH proteolytic substrate.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence including protein accumulation, physical interaction, and in vitro ubiquitination.

claim: Hbp1 accumulates in cells lacking GID/CTLH activity.
source: Indeed, Hbp1 accumulates in cells lacking GID/CTLH activity, and Hbp1 physically interacts and is ubiquitinated in vitro by reconstituted GID/CTLH complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of Hbp1 levels in GID-depleted and GID-KO cells.

claim: Hbp1 physically interacts with the GID/CTLH complex.
source: Indeed, Hbp1 accumulates in cells lacking GID/CTLH activity, and Hbp1 physically interacts and is ubiquitinated in vitro by reconstituted GID/CTLH complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and AP-MS data.

claim: Hbp1 is ubiquitinated in vitro by reconstituted GID/CTLH complexes.
source: Indeed, Hbp1 accumulates in cells lacking GID/CTLH activity, and Hbp1 physically interacts and is ubiquitinated in vitro by reconstituted GID/CTLH complexes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays with purified components.

claim: The GID/CTLH complex prevents cell cycle exit in G1, at least in part by degrading Hbp1.
source: Our biochemical and cellular analysis thus demonstrates that the GID/CTLH complex prevents cell cycle exit in G1, at least in part by degrading Hbp1.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of cell cycle phenotypes and Hbp1 degradation data.

claim: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) degrades roughly 80% of multi-ubiquitinated proteins.
source: A hallmark of proteome balance is the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) that degrades roughly 80% of multi-ubiquitinated proteins (Collins and Goldberg, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Collins and Goldberg, 2017.

claim: In humans, about 600 distinct E3 ubiquitin ligases mark proteins for degradation by 26S proteasomes.
source: In humans, about 600 distinct E3 ubiquitin ligases mark short-lived, malfunctioning and toxic molecules for degradation by 26S proteasomes (Metzger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Metzger et al., 2012.

claim: Perturbations within the ubiquitin-proteasome system are associated with many human diseases, including cancer, neurodegeneration and viral infections.
source: Consistent with the fundamental role of this major cellular quality control nexus, perturbations within the network are associated with many human diseases, including cancer, neurodegeneration and viral infections (Huang and Dixit, 2016; Metzger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Huang and Dixit, 2016 and Metzger et al., 2012.

claim: The yeast GID E3 ligase complex specifically targets gluconeogenic enzymes, including Fbp1, for proteasomal degradation.
source: Particularly in yeast, an organism where gluconeogenesis and glycolytic activity are intermittently coordinated, the multi-subunit GID E3 ligase complex specifically targets the surplus of gluconeogenic enzymes, including the conserved Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (Fbp1), for proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast GID function.

claim: Adequate glucose levels trigger the enzymatic activity of the yeast GID complex by inducing the stabilization and/or de novo synthesis of Gid4.
source: Adequate glucose levels trigger the enzymatic activity of the complex by either inducing the stabilization and/or de novo synthesis of its critical subunit Gid4 (Santt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Santt et al., 2008.

claim: A recent study suggests the presence of a new GID-based constitutive proteolytic pathway termed the Pro/N-end rule pathway.
source: These original findings were broadened by a recent study, suggesting the presence of a new GID-based constitutive proteolytic pathway termed the Pro/N-end rule pathway, wherein N-terminal proline residues and a subsequent stretch of partially flexible amino acids provide the signature for GID-E3 substrate recognition (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: In the Pro/N-end rule pathway, N-terminal proline residues and a subsequent stretch of partially flexible amino acids provide the signature for GID-E3 substrate recognition.
source: These original findings were broadened by a recent study, suggesting the presence of a new GID-based constitutive proteolytic pathway termed the Pro/N-end rule pathway, wherein N-terminal proline residues and a subsequent stretch of partially flexible amino acids provide the signature for GID-E3 substrate recognition (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: In mammals, gluconeogenesis is almost exclusively performed by hepatocytes but also takes place in the kidney cortex and intestine.
source: In mammals, gluconeogenesis is almost exclusively performed by hepatocytes but also takes place, albeit to a much lower extent, in the kidney cortex and intestine (Mutel et al., 2011; Previs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mutel et al., 2011 and Previs et al., 2009.

claim: Maintenance of blood glucose levels during fasting/starvation is primarily achieved through the breakdown of liver glycogen stocks and gluconeogenesis.
source: Indeed, maintenance of blood glucose levels during fasting/starvation and/or rigorous exercise is primarily achieved through the breakdown of liver glycogen stocks (glycogenolysis) and the conversion of non-sugar carbon substrates via gluconeogenesis (Rui, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rui, 2014.

claim: All seven yeast GID proteins have homologous proteins in humans.
source: Nevertheless, all seven yeast GID proteins have homologous proteins in humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sequence homology between yeast and human GID proteins.

claim: RanBP9, Rmnd5, Armc8, Twa1 and MAEA have been found together in a high-molecular weight assembly localized both to the nucleus and cytoplasm, referred to as the CTLH complex.
source: Some of them, RanBP9 (Gid1), Rmnd5 (Gid2), Armc8 (Gid5), Twa1 (Gid8) and MAEA (GID9), have been found together in an ubiquitously expressed high-molecular weight assembly localized both to the nucleus and cytoplasm, also referred to as the C-terminal to LisH (CTLH) complex, after a sequence motif shared between several subunits (Kobayashi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kobayashi et al., 2007.

claim: The counterpart of the yeast regulatory subunit Gid4, c17orf39, was not identified within the mammalian complex in previous studies.
source: However, neither the counterpart of the critical yeast regulatory subunit Gid4, c17orf39, nor the Gid7 sequence homologue, WDR26, were identified within the mammalian complex (Francis et al., 2013; Kobayashi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Francis et al., 2013 and Kobayashi et al., 2007.

claim: The Gid7 sequence homologue, WDR26, was not identified within the mammalian complex in previous studies.
source: However, neither the counterpart of the critical yeast regulatory subunit Gid4, c17orf39, nor the Gid7 sequence homologue, WDR26, were identified within the mammalian complex (Francis et al., 2013; Kobayashi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Francis et al., 2013 and Kobayashi et al., 2007.

claim: Mkln1 was suggested to replace WDR26 in the human GID complex.
source: Instead, Mkln1, a protein involved in cell adhesion and the regulation of cytoskeleton dynamics, was suggested to replace WDR26 in humans (Delto et al., 2015; Francis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Delto et al., 2015 and Francis et al., 2013.

claim: WDR26 was previously identified as a substrate adaptor for the Cullin4-RING ubiquitin ligases (CRL4s).
source: In turn, the WD40-containing protein WDR26 was previously identified as a substrate adaptor for the large family of Cullin4-RING ubiquitin ligases (CRL4s) (Higa et al., 2006; Piwko et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Higa et al., 2006 and Piwko et al., 2010.

claim: RanBP9 was reported to integrate into multiple protein complexes and has numerous interaction partners.
source: RanBP9 was reported to integrate into multiple protein complexes, has numerous interaction partners and was proposed to regulate a diverse set of cellular processes ranging from transcriptional regulation, cell morphology and cell cycle progression to apoptosis (Atabakhsh et al., 2012; Salemi et al., 2017; Suresh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Atabakhsh et al., 2012, Salemi et al., 2017, and Suresh et al., 2012.

claim: WDR26 deletion from RPE cells causes a significant growth inhibition phenotype.
source: To investigate whether the putative CRL4 adapter WDR26 contributes to cellular fitness, we first deleted WDR26 from RPE cells using lentiviral transduction of the CRISPR-Cas9 system and observed a significant growth inhibition phenotype in these cells as judged by clonogenic and MTT assays (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by clonogenic and MTT assays shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: WDR26 is a core part of a protein network encompassing the entire set of homologous S. cerevisiae GID complex subunits.
source: Interestingly, the data exposed WDR26 as a core part of a protein network encompassing the entire set of homologous S. cerevisiae GID complex subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by AP-MS proteomics data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The CRL4 core components Ddb1 and Cullin4A/B were absent or not significantly enriched in WDR26 pull-downs.
source: By contrast, the CRL4 core components Ddb1 and Cullin4A/B were absent or not significantly enriched in WDR26 pull-downs (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by AP-MS data shown in Figure 1—source data 1.

claim: Untagged WDR26 does not associate with the core CRL4 subunit Ddb1 in cells relative to the canonical CRL4 substrate adapter protein WDR23.
source: Consistent with this observation, untagged WDR26 does not associate with the core CRL4 subunit Ddb1 in cells relative to the canonical CRL4 substrate adapter protein WDR23 (DCAF11) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WDR26 is a central subunit of the mammalian GID/CTLH complex.
source: From these results, we conclude that WDR26 is not strongly linked to Cul4 proteins but rather a central subunit of the mammalian GID/CTLH complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteomics and co-IP data showing WDR26 association with GID subunits but not CRL4 components.

claim: The mammalian GID complex comprises ten core components including RanBP9, Rmnd5a, c17ORF39, Armc8, Twa1, MAEA, Mkln1, WDR26, YPEL5, and RanBP10.
source: In accordance with the WDR26 dataset, the largest category of both Rmnd5a- and Armc8-HCIPs comprises the GID members RanBP9 (Gid1), c17ORF39 (Gid4), Armc8 (Gid5), Twa1 (Gid8), MAEA (Gid9) and Mkln1 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Figure 1—source data 2, Figure 1—source data 3). Furthermore, we identified Rmnd5b exclusively in Armc8 and WDR26 samples but not Rmnd5a, suggesting that the presence of the Rmnd5 paralogues in individual GID complexes is mutually exclusive. YPEL5 and RanBP10, a protein highly homologous to RanBP9, also cluster as GID subunits with high probability.
evidence: This is demonstrated by AP-MS experiments and SAINT analysis shown in Figure 1C and related figures.

claim: The presence of Rmnd5 paralogues in individual GID complexes is mutually exclusive.
source: Furthermore, we identified Rmnd5b exclusively in Armc8 and WDR26 samples but not Rmnd5a, suggesting that the presence of the Rmnd5 paralogues in individual GID complexes is mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is inferred from the AP-MS data showing differential presence of Rmnd5a and Rmnd5b.

claim: Native human GID-immunocomplexes purified from HEK-293 cells produce a pronounced ubiquitin smear in in vitro ubiquitination assays.
source: To interrogate a potential E3 ubiquitin ligase function of the human complex, we purified native GID-immunocomplexes from HEK-293 cells and incubated them in the presence of ubiquitin, ATP and a mix of E1 and several E2 enzymes. As shown in Figure 1F, these reactions produced a pronounced ubiquitin smear, which is likely the result of autoubiquitination of one or several subunits in the absence of a cognate substrate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The native human GID complex holds an intrinsic E3 ubiquitin ligase activity.
source: Thus, although residual contaminant E3 ubiquitin ligases in the sample preparation cannot be entirely excluded, these assays provide experimental evidence that the native human GID complex holds an intrinsic E3 ubiquitin ligase activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the ubiquitination assay results, though with a caveat about potential contaminants.

claim: The mammalian GID complex has a molecular weight of ≥550 kDa.
source: With a molecular weight of ≥550 kDa, the mammalian GID complex potentially constitutes an exceptionally large E3 ubiquitin ligase of roughly half the size of the major cell-cycle regulator anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on size estimation from biochemical analysis, with a citation to Zhang et al., 2013 for APC/C comparison.

claim: RanBP9 and WDR26 bind the catalytic body of the E3 ligase, a trimeric complex composed of Rmnd5, MAEA and Twa1.
source: This approach revealed that the conserved proteins RanBP9 and WDR26 bind the catalytic body of the E3 ligase, a trimeric complex composed of the two RING proteins Rmnd5, MAEA and the scaffolding protein Twa1 (Figure 2A and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 2A and E.

claim: The pentameric assembly of RanBP9, WDR26, Rmnd5, MAEA, and Twa1 is catalytically active in autoubiquitination assays.
source: This stable pentameric assembly migrates as an individual peak in size-exclusion experiments, and is also catalytically active in autoubiquitination assays (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by size-exclusion chromatography and autoubiquitination assays shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Twa1 is present as a dimer in the pentameric GID subcomplex.
source: Densitometry quantification of Sypro Ruby-stained gels after gel filtration chromatography suggests a 2:1 molar ratio of Twa1 over the other subunits (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by densitometry analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Isolated untagged Twa1 was found as a constitutive dimer or oligomer.
source: This is consistent with recent data where isolated untagged Twa1 was found as a constitutive dimer or oligomer (Francis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Francis et al., 2017.

claim: SEC-MALS analysis of the pentameric GID complex yielded an average molecular mass of 543 kDa for the first peak, consistent with the formation of a dimer.
source: SEC-MALS yielded two major peaks; the first peak, comprising all five GID proteins, with an average molecular mass of the 543 kDa, is consistent with the formation of a dimer (calculated molecular mass of the pentamer with two molecules of Twa1: ~285 kDa) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In yeast, Gid8 (Twa1 homologue) is the central hub connecting the RING dimer to Gid1 (RanBP9) and Gid7 (WDR26).
source: In yeast, deletion analysis to map Gid-Gid protein interactions identified the homologue of Twa1, Gid8, as the central hub connecting the RING dimer to the proteins Gid1 (RanBP9) and Gid7 (WDR26) (Menssen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Menssen et al., 2012.

claim: Twa1 is pivotal for efficient MAEA and Rmnd5a RING dimerization and downstream recruitment of peripheral members of the protein complex in vitro.
source: Similarly, within the human complex, Twa1 is pivotal for efficient MAEA and Rmnd5a RING dimerization and downstream recruitment of the peripheral members of the protein complex in vitro (Figure 2E and data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Depletion of Twa1 in HEK-293 cells leads to disruption of the GID complex.
source: Together, the reconstitution data strongly predict cellular disintegration of the complex in the absence of the core protein Twa1. Indeed, when the complex was purified by immunoprecipitation from HEK-293 cells depleted for Twa1 using a pool of siRNAs, the otherwise stable GID network was largely disrupted (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments in Twa1-depleted cells shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The pentameric core GID proteins form the platform required for downstream recruitment of Mkln1, YPEL5 and an independent unit formed by Armc8 and GID4.
source: Furthermore, step-wise in vitro reconstitution of the entire complex revealed that the pentameric core GID proteins form the platform strictly required for the downstream recruitment of the metazoan-specific protein Mkln1, YPEL5 and an independent unit formed by Armc8 and GID4 wherein GID4 only incorporates into the complex in the presence of Armc8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by step-wise in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: GID4 only incorporates into the complex in the presence of Armc8.
source: Furthermore, step-wise in vitro reconstitution of the entire complex revealed that the pentameric core GID proteins form the platform strictly required for the downstream recruitment of the metazoan-specific protein Mkln1, YPEL5 and an independent unit formed by Armc8 and GID4 wherein GID4 only incorporates into the complex in the presence of Armc8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by step-wise in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: Both WDR26 and Mkln1 coexist within a single GID complex.
source: Notably, both previously proposed yeast Gid7 homologues, WDR26 and Mkln1, coexist within a single GID complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When the hGID complex was mixed with Ube2H, a striking increase in autocatalytic hGID activity was observed.
source: Remarkably, when the hGID complex was mixed with Ube2H, a striking increase in autocatalytic hGID activity was observed, and ubiquitin was preferentially transferred to the RING protein MAEA (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Ubiquitin was preferentially transferred to the RING protein MAEA in Ube2H-dependent ubiquitination assays.
source: Remarkably, when the hGID complex was mixed with Ube2H, a striking increase in autocatalytic hGID activity was observed, and ubiquitin was preferentially transferred to the RING protein MAEA (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 2H.

claim: No GID E3 ligase activity was detected with E2 enzymes including UbcH5 family and Cdc34.
source: No such activity was detected with any of the other tested E2 enzymes, including the promiscuous UbcH5 family and the SCF-specific E2 Cdc34 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ube2H peptides were exclusively found in Armc8- and WDR26-immunoprecipitates.
source: These data are supported by the presence of Ube2H peptides exclusively in Armc8- and WDR26-immunoprecipitates (Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 1—source data 3), and a weak but reproducible association of recombinant Ube2H and the hGID core complex in FLAG-based pulldown assays (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by AP-MS data and FLAG pulldown assays.

claim: Ube2H displays 54% amino acid sequence identity to the yeast E2 Ubc8/Gid3.
source: Notably, Ube2H displays 54% amino acid sequence identity to the yeast E2 Ubc8/Gid3, which is required to degrade gluconeogenic enzymes (Kaiser et al., 1994; Schüle et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison, with citations to Kaiser et al., 1994 and Schüle et al., 2000.

claim: Ubc8/Gid3 is required to degrade gluconeogenic enzymes in yeast.
source: Notably, Ube2H displays 54% amino acid sequence identity to the yeast E2 Ubc8/Gid3, which is required to degrade gluconeogenic enzymes (Kaiser et al., 1994; Schüle et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kaiser et al., 1994 and Schüle et al., 2000.

claim: MAEA-deficient cells show a remarkable decrease in their proliferative capacity compared to control cells.
source: Like WDR26-KOs, MAEA-deficient cells are characterized by a remarkable decrease in their proliferative capacity compared to cells treated with control gRNA in MTT and clonogenic assays (Figure 3A and C, data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT and clonogenic assays shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: Deletion of the RING protein MAEA renders the GID ligase inactive.
source: As expected, deletion of the RING protein renders the ligase inactive and results in altered GID complex assembly and subunit stabilization, suggesting an autoregulatory mechanism frequently observed for E3 ligases (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) (Metzger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Deletion of MAEA results in altered GID complex assembly and subunit stabilization.
source: As expected, deletion of the RING protein renders the ligase inactive and results in altered GID complex assembly and subunit stabilization, suggesting an autoregulatory mechanism frequently observed for E3 ligases (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) (Metzger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mitotic marker phospho-Histone H3 (Ser10) was absent in MAEA- and WDR26-KO cells.
source: Immunoblotting of cell extracts revealed that the mitotic marker phospho-Histone H3 (Ser10) was absent in MAEA- and WDR26-KO cells (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The decrease in cell proliferation in GID-KO cells was not due to an increment in apoptotic cell death.
source: Furthermore, the decrease in cell proliferation was not due to an increment in apoptotic cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), but is manifested by a pronounced downregulation of both the levels and phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein (Rb) and of several other cell cycle markers including Cyclin A and to a lower extent Cyclin D1 (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GID-KO cells show pronounced downregulation of both the levels and phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein (Rb).
source: Furthermore, the decrease in cell proliferation was not due to an increment in apoptotic cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), but is manifested by a pronounced downregulation of both the levels and phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein (Rb) and of several other cell cycle markers including Cyclin A and to a lower extent Cyclin D1 (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Phosphorylation of nuclear pRB by CDKs is crucial for cell cycle entry to unleash the activities of growth-promoting transcription factors such as the E2F family.
source: In agreement with these observations, phosphorylation of nuclear pRB by CDKs is known to be crucial for cell cycle entry to unleash the activities of growth-promoting transcription factors such as the E2F family (Brown et al., 1999; Rizzolio et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown et al., 1999 and Rizzolio et al., 2012.

claim: GID-KO cells adapt within days of culturing, restoring normal cell proliferation.
source: Curiously, cells lacking hGID activity adapt within days of culturing, restoring normal cell proliferation (Figure 3C), accompanied by re-expression of all cell cycle markers that are nearly indistinguishable to control cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MTT assays and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Adapted GID-KO cells show re-expression of all cell cycle markers that are nearly indistinguishable to control cells.
source: Curiously, cells lacking hGID activity adapt within days of culturing, restoring normal cell proliferation (Figure 3C), accompanied by re-expression of all cell cycle markers that are nearly indistinguishable to control cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: GID-KO cells rapidly acquire suppressor mutations and/or activate a compensatory pro-proliferative transcriptional program.
source: Thus, we speculate that GID-KO cells rapidly acquire suppressor mutations and/or activate a compensatory pro-proliferative transcriptional program that overrides the loss of hGID-activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed adaptation phenotype.

claim: Most human gluconeogenic enzymes do not harbor N-terminal proline residues.
source: Surprisingly, most human gluconeogenic enzymes do not harbor N-terminal proline residues, which was recently postulated as main recognition motif for the yeast GID E3-ligase (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis, with a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: FBP1 levels remained unchanged in MAEA-KO cells under normal growth conditions.
source: The relative abundance of the gluconeogenic enzyme FBP1 was first assayed in RPE and HEK-293 cells lacking GID activity under normal growth condition. Indeed, we found that FBP1 levels remained unchanged in MAEA-KO cells, in contrast to the autoregulated hGID subunit YPEL5 (Figure 3E, data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The autoregulated hGID subunit YPEL5 is stabilized in MAEA-KO cells.
source: Indeed, we found that FBP1 levels remained unchanged in MAEA-KO cells, in contrast to the autoregulated hGID subunit YPEL5 (Figure 3E, data not shown).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: mFBP1 and mPCK1 protein levels remained relatively stable over the time-course and unresponsive to GID knockdown during metabolic switch.
source: Unlike yFbp1 and yPck1, which are rapidly degraded in the presence of glucose in a GID-dependent manner (Chen et al., 2017), mFBP1 and mPCK1 protein levels remained relatively stable over the time-course and unresponsive to GID knockdown.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis of metabolic switch experiments shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: yFbp1 and yPck1 are rapidly degraded in the presence of glucose in a GID-dependent manner.
source: Unlike yFbp1 and yPck1, which are rapidly degraded in the presence of glucose in a GID-dependent manner (Chen et al., 2017), mFBP1 and mPCK1 protein levels remained relatively stable over the time-course and unresponsive to GID knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: FBP1 mRNA levels drop after shifting cells from a fasted to a fed state irrespective of the presence of the GID complex in primary hepatocytes.
source: Moreover, FBP1 mRNA levels drop after shifting cells from a fasted to a fed state irrespective of the presence of the GID complex in primary hepatocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Knockdown of GID did not alter glucose production or glucose levels when primary hepatocytes were shifted from gluconeogenesis to glycolysis.
source: Additionally, knockdown of GID did not alter glucose production or glucose levels when primary hepatocytes were shifted from gluconeogenesis to glycolysis as would be expected if the GID complex takes on the same function as in yeast (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by glucose production and glucose level measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Neither mammalian FBP1 nor PCK1 are targets of the GID complex.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that neither mammalian FBP1 nor PCK1 are targets of the GID complex, indicating a substantial functional divergence of the GID E3 ligase between yeast and mammals.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolic switch experiments showing no effect of GID depletion on FBP1 and PCK1 levels.

claim: There is substantial functional divergence of the GID E3 ligase between yeast and mammals.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that neither mammalian FBP1 nor PCK1 are targets of the GID complex, indicating a substantial functional divergence of the GID E3 ligase between yeast and mammals.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of conservation of gluconeogenic enzyme degradation function.

claim: The conserved HTRA2 protease emerged as a strong interactor of the GID complex.
source: While the GET complex subunit BAG6 was only weakly detectable in GID-immunocomplexes, the conserved HTRA2 protease emerged as a strong interactor (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HTRA2 was initially proposed to function as a pro-apoptotic molecule inducing cell death under adverse growth conditions.
source: This serine protease was initially proposed to function as a pro-apoptotic molecule inducing cell death under adverse growth conditions, but was recently found to generally contribute to cellular homeostasis (Kuninaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kuninaka et al., 2007.

claim: HTRA2 levels did not significantly change in MAEA or WDR26 deleted cells.
source: Consistent with the MS-data, we did not observe a significant change in HTRA2 levels in MAEA or WDR26 deleted HEK-293 or HeLa Kyoto cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), implying that HTRA2 is unlikely a proteolytic GID substrate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HTRA2 is unlikely a proteolytic GID substrate.
source: Consistent with the MS-data, we did not observe a significant change in HTRA2 levels in MAEA or WDR26 deleted HEK-293 or HeLa Kyoto cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), implying that HTRA2 is unlikely a proteolytic GID substrate.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of HTRA2 stabilization in GID-KO cells.

claim: Hbp1 is strongly enriched in MG132-treated samples.
source: Next, we focused our analysis on the high mobility group (HMG) box-containing protein 1 (Hbp1), which is strongly enriched in MG132-treated samples (Figure 4C), indicative of a UPS-regulated interaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by AP-MS data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Hbp1 was previously reported to regulate the expression of important cell cycle regulators such as N-Myc, Cyclin D1, p16 and p21.
source: Hbp1 was previously reported to regulate the expression of important cell cycle regulators such as N-Myc, Cyclin D1, p16 and p21, thereby triggering a slowdown of cell growth and premature senescence (Li et al., 2010; Sampson et al., 2001; Tevosian et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2010, Sampson et al., 2001, Tevosian et al., 1997, and Wang et al., 2012.

claim: Hbp1 triggers a slowdown of cell growth and premature senescence.
source: Hbp1 was previously reported to regulate the expression of important cell cycle regulators such as N-Myc, Cyclin D1, p16 and p21, thereby triggering a slowdown of cell growth and premature senescence (Li et al., 2010; Sampson et al., 2001; Tevosian et al., 1997; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2010, Sampson et al., 2001, Tevosian et al., 1997, and Wang et al., 2012.

claim: Hbp1-immunoprecipitates comprise its known binding partner and transcriptional corepressor Sin3A and the GID subunits RanBP9 and MAEA.
source: Indeed, Hbp1-immunoprecipitates comprise its known binding partner and transcriptional corepressor Sin3A and the GID subunits RanBP9 and MAEA (Figure 4E) (Swanson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4E, with a citation to Swanson et al., 2004.

claim: AP-MS of Hbp1 recovered two large functional clusters, encompassing multiple subunits of the Sin3A corepressor complex and the entire set of human GID subunits.
source: Moreover, AP-MS followed by SAINT analysis recovered two large functional clusters, encompassing multiple subunits of the Sin3A corepressor complex and the entire set of human GID subunits (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by AP-MS and SAINT analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The GID complex predominantly accumulates in the nucleus.
source: Since the GID complex predominantly accumulates in the nucleus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), together these results support the hypothesis that the GID complex might target nuclear Hbp1 for proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hbp1 levels increased approximately 3-fold across all cell types tested upon downregulation of different GID subunits.
source: Remarkably, Hbp1 levels increased approximately 3-fold across all cell types tested (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A and B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Hbp1 mRNA levels quantified by qRT-PCR in GID-depleted cells are comparable to controls.
source: In contrast, Hbp1 mRNA levels quantified by qRT-PCR in GID-depleted cells are comparable to controls (Figure 5C), excluding the possibility that elevated Hbp1 levels are indirectly caused by upregulated Hbp1 transcription.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Complementation assays with inducible expression of a RNAi-resistant version of WDR26 confirmed that Hbp1 stabilization is a direct consequence of crippled GID activity.
source: Complementation assays with inducible expression of a RNAi-resistant version of WDR26 confirmed that Hbp1 stabilization is a direct consequence of crippled GID activity (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by complementation experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Hbp1 levels were upregulated in both WDR26-KO and MAEA-KO cells accompanied with a slightly reduced expression of Cyclin D1.
source: Moreover, Hbp1 levels were also upregulated in both WDR26-KO and MAEA-KO cells accompanied with a slightly reduced expression of Cyclin D1, a presumed Hbp1 transcriptional target (Figure 5E) (Sampson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5E, with a citation to Sampson et al., 2001.

claim: Total Cyclin D1 mRNA was partially repressed in WDR26-KO cells.
source: Consistent with this observation, we found total Cyclin D1 mRNA partially repressed in WDR26-KO cells, correlating in intensity with ectopic overexpression of Hbp1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: The lack of WDR26 strongly reduced the rate of Hbp1 degradation.
source: Notably, the lack of WDR26 strongly reduced the rate of Hbp1 degradation (Figure 5F), suggesting that the complex is required for Hbp1 degradation in vivo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The GID complex is required for Hbp1 degradation in vivo.
source: Notably, the lack of WDR26 strongly reduced the rate of Hbp1 degradation (Figure 5F), suggesting that the complex is required for Hbp1 degradation in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the cycloheximide chase experiments showing reduced Hbp1 degradation in WDR26-depleted cells.

claim: The human GID substrate Hbp1 contains an alternative start site that conforms to a perfect yeast GID Pro/N-end rule recognition motif.
source: Intriguingly, we noticed that the human GID substrate Hbp1 contains an alternative start site just 10 amino acids downstream of its canonical sequence that conforms to a perfect yeast GID Pro/N-end rule recognition motif (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis, with a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: The Hbp1-P11G mutant was degraded with kinetics similar to the wild-type protein.
source: However, the Hbp1-P11G mutant was degraded with kinetics similar to the wild-type protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), arguing against a conserved Pro/N-end rule pathway consensus targeting sequence for the case of Hbp1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: A conserved Pro/N-end rule pathway consensus targeting sequence is not required for Hbp1 degradation.
source: However, the Hbp1-P11G mutant was degraded with kinetics similar to the wild-type protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), arguing against a conserved Pro/N-end rule pathway consensus targeting sequence for the case of Hbp1.
evidence: This is inferred from the P11G mutant degradation data.

claim: Hbp1 was specifically ubiquitinated by hGID but not by the control E3 ligase CRL4CRBN in vitro.
source: Indeed, Hbp1 was specifically ubiquitinated by hGID but not by the control E3 ligase CRL4CRBN (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 5F (note: there appears to be a figure reference error in the manuscript, should be 5G).

claim: The human GID complex was unable to detect ubiquitinated yFbp1 in in vitro ubiquitination assays.
source: However, although we observed GID autoubiquitination, we were unable to detect ubiquitinated yFbp1 in these experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Hbp1 is a proteolytic substrate of the human GID E3 ligase complex.
source: Together, these data establish that Hbp1 is a proteolytic substrate of the human GID E3 ligase complex, and indicate that degradation of Hbp1 might be required for efficient cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence including protein accumulation, interaction, and in vitro ubiquitination.

claim: Degradation of Hbp1 might be required for efficient cell proliferation.
source: Together, these data establish that Hbp1 is a proteolytic substrate of the human GID E3 ligase complex, and indicate that degradation of Hbp1 might be required for efficient cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of Hbp1 degradation data and cell proliferation phenotypes.

claim: The catalytic core of the human GID complex is compositely formed by the RING proteins MAEA and either Rmnd5a or its paralog Rmnd5b.
source: First, the catalytic core is compositely formed by the RING proteins MAEA and either Rmnd5a or its paralog Rmnd5b (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the reconstitution experiments and summarized in Figure 6A.

claim: RING dimerization is a functional requirement of several non-catalytic RING E3 ligases to stabilize the E2 ~ubiquitin thioester bond for ubiquitin transfer.
source: Interestingly, RING dimerization is a functional requirement of several non-catalytic RING E3 ligases to stabilize the E2 ~ubiquitin thioester bond for ubiquitin transfer. Dimerization can be either mediated by the RING domain alone or facilitated by flanking helical regions (Berndsen and Wolberger, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berndsen and Wolberger, 2014.

claim: Optimal RING association in the GID complex is dependent on the small scaffolding protein Twa1.
source: Interestingly, for the GID complex, we observed that optimal RING association is dependent on the small scaffolding protein Twa1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: Twa1 itself dimerizes to form a central hub for the downstream recruitment of the core and peripheral members of the protein complex.
source: Our data additionally suggest that Twa1 itself dimerizes to form a central hub for the downstream recruitment of the core and peripheral members of the protein complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the stoichiometry and reconstitution data.

claim: In yeast, Gid4 association is tightly regulated and the protein acts both as substrate adapter for gluconeogenic enzymes as well as an activator of the E3 ligase activity.
source: In yeast, Gid4 association is tightly regulated and the protein acts both as substrate adapter for gluconeogenic enzymes as well as an activator of the E3 ligase activity (Chen et al., 2017; Santt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2017 and Santt et al., 2008.

claim: The human GID complex without the Armc8/GID4-module efficiently cooperates with Ube2H in autoubiquitination assays in vitro.
source: However, our data suggest that at least in vitro the human GID complex without the Armc8/GID4-module efficiently cooperates with Ube2H in autoubiquitination assays.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in vitro ubiquitination assays with subcomplexes.

claim: The highly homologous proteins RanBP9 and RanBP10 may co-reside in individual GID complexes.
source: For example, it remains open if the highly homologous proteins RanBP9 and RanBP10 co-reside in individual complexes as suggested by our proteomics data.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proteomics data.

claim: In mammals, gluconeogenesis is largely restricted to hepatocytes and only activated upon extended periods of fasting.
source: Compared to unicellular organisms, higher eukaryotes are highly specialized within tissues and organs in their internal biochemistry. Gluconeogenesis is largely restricted to hepatocytes and only activated upon extended periods of fasting.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian metabolism.

claim: The GID complex is ubiquitously expressed.
source: However, the GID complex is ubiquitously expressed, pointing towards an extended substrate repertoire, possibly depending on the prevailing cellular milieu and/or metabolic programs of different cell types.
evidence: This is based on the observation that GID is found in multiple cell types.

claim: All identified yeast GID substrates to date have proline residues in the first or second position after their start methionine.
source: Notably, a shared feature of all identified yeast GID substrates to date are proline residues in the first or second position after their start methionine and the presence of this amino acid is critical for GID-mediated degradation (Menssen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Menssen et al., 2012.

claim: The substrate-binding pocket of yeast and human Gid4 is highly conserved.
source: Indeed, the substrate-binding pocket of yeast and human Gid4 is highly conserved and human GID4 is able to recognize and bind various proline-containing N-degrons (Dong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2018.

claim: Human GID4 is able to recognize and bind various proline-containing N-degrons.
source: Indeed, the substrate-binding pocket of yeast and human Gid4 is highly conserved and human GID4 is able to recognize and bind various proline-containing N-degrons (Dong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2018.

claim: The hGID-substrate Hbp1 does not possess a proline-containing N-degron.
source: However, the hGID-substrate Hbp1 identified here does not possess a proline-containing N-degron.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of Hbp1.

claim: GID4 is more loosely associated with the complex than other subunits.
source: Since our AP-MS data suggest that GID4 is more loosely associated with the complex than other subunits (Figure 1—source data 2, Figure 1—source data 3), we speculate that different mechanisms for regulated substrate recruitment may exist for mammalian GID E3 ligase complexes.
evidence: This is based on AP-MS data shown in Figure 1—source data 2 and 3.

claim: Different mechanisms for regulated substrate recruitment may exist for mammalian GID E3 ligase complexes.
source: Since our AP-MS data suggest that GID4 is more loosely associated with the complex than other subunits (Figure 1—source data 2, Figure 1—source data 3), we speculate that different mechanisms for regulated substrate recruitment may exist for mammalian GID E3 ligase complexes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the GID4 association data and Hbp1 substrate characteristics.

claim: RanBP9-KO mice revealed that this GID subunit is critical for early embryonic development.
source: Analyses of RanBP9-KO mice revealed that this GID subunit is critical for early embryonic development, but some pups survive and are significantly smaller than their wild-type littermates (Palavicini et al., 2013; Puverel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Palavicini et al., 2013 and Puverel et al., 2011.

claim: Some RanBP9-KO pups survive and are significantly smaller than their wild-type littermates.
source: Analyses of RanBP9-KO mice revealed that this GID subunit is critical for early embryonic development, but some pups survive and are significantly smaller than their wild-type littermates (Palavicini et al., 2013; Puverel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Palavicini et al., 2013 and Puverel et al., 2011.

claim: Individual deletions of critical GID subunits result in proliferation defects in several cell lines.
source: Available evidence suggests that individual deletions of critical GID subunits, such as the RING protein MAEA and the structural integrity protein Twa1, result in proliferation defects in several cell lines (Hart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hart et al., 2015.

claim: The hGID complex is not essential for cell proliferation per se.
source: While at present we do not know the molecular mechanisms underlying this suppression, we conclude that the hGID complex is not essential for cell proliferation per se, but negatively regulates one or several cell cycle inhibitors, possibly involved in cell cycle exit.
evidence: This is inferred from the adaptation phenotype of GID-KO cells.

claim: The hGID complex negatively regulates one or several cell cycle inhibitors, possibly involved in cell cycle exit.
source: While at present we do not know the molecular mechanisms underlying this suppression, we conclude that the hGID complex is not essential for cell proliferation per se, but negatively regulates one or several cell cycle inhibitors, possibly involved in cell cycle exit.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle phenotypes and Hbp1 substrate identification.

claim: Hbp1 was proposed to function as a tumor suppressor.
source: Interestingly, our targeted AP-MS experiments identified the transcription factor Hbp1 as a proteolytic target of the E3 ligase in various human cell lines (Figure 6B). Hbp1 was proposed to function as a tumor suppressor and has been implicated in regulating cell cycle exit.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hbp1 function.

claim: Cells overexpressing Hbp1 were previously shown to enter a quiescent-like G0 state.
source: Indeed, cells overexpressing Hbp1 were previously shown to enter a quiescent-like G0 state (Shih et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shih et al., 2001.

claim: Hbp1 directly binds high-affinity elements on negatively regulated target genes, including N-Myc and DNMT1.
source: Molecularly, Hbp1 executes dual transcriptional functions by directly binding high-affinity elements on negatively regulated target genes, including N-Myc and DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1), but also transcriptionally activates genes, such as p16, p21 and histone H1 (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2013.

claim: Hbp1 transcriptionally activates genes, such as p16, p21 and histone H1.
source: Molecularly, Hbp1 executes dual transcriptional functions by directly binding high-affinity elements on negatively regulated target genes, including N-Myc and DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1), but also transcriptionally activates genes, such as p16, p21 and histone H1 (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2013.

claim: The majority of Hbp1 is tightly embedded into a multi-subunit Sin3a corepressor complex.
source: Interestingly, our proteomic data suggest that the majority of Hbp1 is tightly embedded into a multi-subunit Sin3a corepressor complex.
evidence: This is based on AP-MS data showing Hbp1 interaction with Sin3a complex subunits.

claim: Sin3a-related proteins are excluded from the GID-interactome.
source: However, in sharp contrast to Hbp1, Sin3a-related proteins are excluded from the GID-interactome.
evidence: This is based on AP-MS data of GID subunits.

claim: Continuous GID-mediated proteolytic clearance of Hbp1 in cycling cells is installed to avert the assembly of a repressor complex that controls the expression of a set of anti-proliferative genes.
source: Therefore, it is conceivable that continuous GID-mediated proteolytic clearance of Hbp1 in cycling cells is installed to avert the assembly of a repressor complex that controls the expression of a set of anti-proliferative genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the combination of Hbp1 function and GID-mediated degradation.

claim: Yeast Moh1 is dispensable for catalytic GID activity.
source: However, Moh1-deficient cells degrade TAP-tagged Fbp1 with wild-type kinetics, whereas - as expected - Fbp1 levels remain high in cells lacking Gid4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F). We thus conclude that the yeast YPEL5, Moh1, is dispensable for catalytic GID activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Fbp1 degradation assays in moh1Δ cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of the human GID complex is evolutionary conserved.
source: Moreover, we identified additional human GID subunits and demonstrate that the E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of this multi-subunit complex is evolutionary conserved.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the in vitro reconstitution and ubiquitination assays.

claim: Cellular GID activity is critical for maintenance of normal cell proliferation rates.
source: Finally, we provide evidence that cellular GID activity is critical for maintenance of normal cell proliferation rates, possibly by direct ubiquitination of the transcription factor Hbp1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the proliferation assays in GID-KO cells.
